results.summary: This project displays a four-frame spinner animation on a 7-segment LED display while also demonstrating basic logic gates. It is divided into two subprojects: one shows the animation automatically, and the other lets users toggle DIP switches to see the effects of wire, NOT, AND, and OR gates. External hardware includes a 7-segment LED display and DIP switches. The design is a simple educational example created in Wokwi, with no silicon test results reported.

This design implements four instances of a 2:1 multiplexer with differential outputs, aiming to minimize logic hazards. The multiplexer inputs and select line are exposed on the input pins, while the differential outputs are on the output pins. The documentation is mostly a template and does not explain how the hazard minimization is achieved or how to test the design. No external hardware or silicon results are mentioned.

This project displays the name of the author's dog one character at a time on a 7-segment display. It uses a clock and reset input, along with two additional inputs, and drives six output pins connected to the display segments. The documentation is a template with no explanation of how the design works or how to test it. No external hardware or silicon results are described.

This project implements a pseudo-random number generator that produces numbers from 1 to 6, simulating a dice roll. It has seven input pins and eight output pins, likely for buttons and a 7-segment display, but the documentation is a template with no functional description. The design is intended for a Tiny Tapeout workshop submission. No external hardware or silicon results are mentioned.

This is a copy of the Tiny Tapeout template, described as a first quick revision. It contains no documentation beyond the template placeholders, so its functionality is unknown. No pins, external hardware, or test results are provided. It appears to be an initial submission with no specific design implemented.

This is an experimental XOR test project created during a Tiny Tapeout workshop. The documentation is entirely template text, so the exact implementation and usage are not described. No pins, external hardware, or test results are provided. It serves as a basic logic experiment for educational purposes.

This project is a simple 6-bit shift register with toggle-enabled feedback, created for a Tiny Tapeout workshop. It has a clock, reset, and two data inputs, and outputs six bits. The documentation is a template with no explanation of how the feedback works or how to test it. No external hardware or silicon results are mentioned.

This design spins segments around a 7-segment display and can reverse direction. It uses D flip-flops with reset to sequence the outer six segments (A-F), with a multiplexer controlled by input IN0 to stop the sequence after six shifts. Reversing is done by multiplexers switching the flip-flop outputs to the display, and reset clears the display. External hardware includes switches for IN0 and IN1 and a 7-segment display for outputs OUT0 to OUT5.

This project implements a 128-bit SRAM using D flip-flops, address decoders, and multiplexers. It has three address bits, eight bidirectional data pins, and a read/write control, with outputs also driving a 7-segment display. To test, users connect address and data pins, set R/W high and clock to write, or set R/W low to read without clocking. External hardware may include a 7-segment display or LEDs, and bidirectional tristate buffers for the data pins.

This project creates an LED chaser with random direction changes and blinks, driving a 7-segment display. It uses a single clock input and eight segment outputs. The documentation is a template with no explanation of how the random direction changes are generated or how to test the design. No external hardware or silicon results are mentioned.
